title: Interleaving String
description: Brute force to optimized: exponential backtracking versus a 2D dynamic programming table versus a rolling 1D array.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given three strings s1, s2, and s3, determine whether s3 can be formed by interleaving the characters of s1 and s2, while preserving the relative order of characters within each of s1 and s2.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given three strings s1, s2, and s3, determine whether s3 can be formed by interleaving the characters of s1 and s2, while preserving the relative order of characters within each of s1 and s2.

blocks.title: Analogy: Riffle Shuffling Two Card Decks Into One
blocks.text: Like riffle shuffling two separate decks of cards together into a single pile: cards from each original deck keep their own internal order, but they can be interleaved with each other in any pattern.

blocks.caption: Merge two strings, preserving each one's own internal order, to form a third

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s1 = "aabcc", s2 = "dbbca", s3 = "aadbbcbcac"

blocks.text: Edge case: s1 and s2 both empty
If s1 and s2 are both empty, the only valid interleaving is also an empty string, so this is true only if s3 is empty too, otherwise false.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether the recursive choice at each step ever leads back to a situation already explored.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Wildcard Matching already showed that when a recursion revisits the exact same pair of positions repeatedly, through different sequences of earlier choices, a 2D table computes each pair's answer exactly once instead of re-exploring it.

Observation 2: Here, the pair worth tracking is how many characters have been consumed from s1 and how many from s2, since together they always determine exactly which character of s3 comes next, at position i plus j.

Observation 3: A cell dp[i][j] is true exactly when either the character just before it came validly from s1 (dp[i minus 1][j] was true, and s1's next character matches) or from s2 (dp[i][j minus 1] was true, and s2's next character matches), the same two branches the brute force recursion tried, just computed once each.

Observation 4: Tracing s1 equal to "ab", s2 equal to "cd", s3 equal to "acbd" through the table confirms it, converging cell by cell to dp[2][2] true, correctly identifying the valid interleaving a (from s1), c (from s2), b (from s1), d (from s2).

Recognizing that the recursion revisits identical (characters consumed from s1, characters consumed from s2) pairs is what turns exponential backtracking into a 2D table computed once, cell by cell, exactly as with Wildcard Matching.
6. Brute Force Solution

Recursively try both choices at every step: take the next character from s1, or take the next character from s2, provided it matches the next required character of s3, backtracking whenever a choice leads to a dead end.
Step by step algorithm

items: If both s1 and s2 are fully consumed, check whether s3 is also fully consumed.
If the next character of s1 matches the next required character of s3, recursively try consuming it.
If the next character of s2 also matches, recursively try consuming it as well.
Succeed if either recursive path succeeds.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The upfront length check rejects any case where s3's length does not equal the combined length of s1 and s2, since no interleaving could ever produce a mismatched total length.
At every position, the position within s3 to match against is always i plus j, since exactly that many characters have been consumed in total from s1 and s2 combined.
Either branch succeeding is sufficient, since the two are independent ways of accounting for the same next character of s3.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible way of weaving s1 and s2 together is explored, so a valid interleaving is always found if one exists.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential in the worst case, since each position branches into up to two recursive calls.
Space: O(n plus m), for the recursion call stack.

Limitation: the same (i, j) position pair, representing how much of s1 and s2 have been consumed so far, can be reached through many different orderings of choices, and each time it is reached the same remaining work gets redone from scratch.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: the same (i, j) pair of consumed lengths can be reached through many different orderings of s1 and s2 choices, and each arrival redoes identical remaining work.

What a 2D table fixes directly: storing whether the first i characters of s1 and first j characters of s2 can interleave to form the first i plus j characters of s3, computed once per pair, eliminates every repeated recomputation.

How each cell is filled: it is true if either the cell above (one more character consumed from s1, matching) or the cell to the left (one more character consumed from s2, matching) is true, mirroring the brute force's two branches exactly.

The core idea: fill the table row by row, so every (i, j) pair is computed exactly once, using only the cell above and the cell to the left.

Build a two dimensional table where dp[i][j] represents whether the first i characters of s1 and the first j characters of s2 can interleave to form the first i plus j characters of s3. Each cell depends only on the cell directly above it (consuming one more character from s1) and the cell directly to its left (consuming one more character from s2), so every distinct state is computed exactly once.
9. Optimized Solution
A 2D table filled row by row, where each cell checks whether the next character could have come from s1 or from s2.
Dry run for s1 = "ab", s2 = "cd", s3 = "acbd"

blocks.caption: Optimized: a 2D table where each cell checks whether s1 or s2 could supply the next character

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because dp[i][j] is built entirely from strictly smaller, already computed states, either the cell above (one more character from s1) or the cell to the left (one more character from s2), so by the time the table reaches dp[n][m], every possible way s1 and s2 could interleave to reach that exact combined length has already been correctly accounted for.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The next character of s3 matches s1's next character, and the shorter prefix already interleaved successfully","dp[i][j] becomes true via the cell directly above it","This path correctly credits s1 with supplying the current character"],["The next character of s3 matches s2's next character, and the shorter prefix already interleaved successfully","dp[i][j] becomes true via the cell directly to its left","This path correctly credits s2 with supplying the current character"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m), filling every cell of the table exactly once.
Space: O(n times m), for the full table.
10. Further Optimization: Rolling the Table Into One Row

Every cell only depends on the cell directly above it and the cell directly to its left, both of which belong to either the current row or the immediately preceding row. This means the full 2D table can be collapsed into a single 1D array updated left to right, one row at a time, reducing the space to be proportional to only the shorter of the two source strings.

codes.python:
def is_interleave(s1, s2, s3):
    n, m = len(s1), len(s2)
    if n + m != len(s3):
        return False
    dp = [False] * (m + 1)
    dp[0] = True
    for j in range(1, m + 1):
        dp[j] = dp[j - 1] and s2[j - 1] == s3[j - 1]
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        dp[0] = dp[0] and s1[i - 1] == s3[i - 1]
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            k = i + j - 1
            from_s1 = dp[j] and s1[i - 1] == s3[k]                      # reuses last row's value, still in dp[j]
            from_s2 = dp[j - 1] and s2[j - 1] == s3[k]                    # this row's already updated value
            dp[j] = from_s1 or from_s2
    return dp[m]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s1 = "ab"
    s2 = "cd"
    s3 = "acbd"
    print(is_interleave(s1, s2, s3))

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Before processing a new row, the value at dp[0] is updated in place to reflect whether the growing prefix of s1 alone still matches the corresponding prefix of s3.
While scanning across a row, dp[j] still holds the previous row's value (the cell above) until it is overwritten, so it can be read for the "came from s1" case before being replaced.
The "came from s2" case reads dp[j minus 1], which belongs to the current row and has already been updated earlier in this same pass, exactly mirroring the cell to the left.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m), unchanged.
Space: O(m), a single rolling row instead of the full table.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

This is another two dimensional string DP where every cell's dependency stays within the current and immediately previous row, making it a natural candidate for the same rolling array space reduction used elsewhere.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the quick length check up front (length of s1 plus length of s2 must equal length of s3), which immediately rules out impossible cases.
Mixing up whether dp[i][j] represents characters consumed or an index, leading to off by one errors when indexing into s3.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["One of s1 or s2 being empty","The answer reduces to simply checking whether the other string equals s3 exactly."],["Overlapping characters between s1 and s2 at the same position","The brute force and DP both handle this correctly since they check actual index alignment, not just character presence."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

State the base cases (dp[0][0], the first row, and the first column) explicitly before filling the rest of the table, since getting these initial conditions wrong is the most common source of bugs in this exact problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the exponential blowup", think: a 2D table memoizing every (characters consumed from s1, characters consumed from s2) pair exactly once.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce the space used", think: roll the table into a single row, since each row only depends on the one directly above it.
If the interviewer says "what if s1 and s2 could overlap in content", think: the DP already handles this correctly, since it tracks index positions, not just which characters exist.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does dp[i][j] only ever need to check the cell above and the cell to the left, never any other cell?
How would you reconstruct one actual valid interleaving, not just determine whether one exists?
How would this approach extend to interleaving three or more source strings instead of just two?
Why can the table be rolled into a single row, and what has to be updated carefully to make that safe?
How would you count the total number of distinct valid interleavings, rather than just checking whether one exists?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Wildcard Matching, whose 2D table and rolling array reduction follow the exact same structure, just with a different rule for what each cell checks.
Climbing Stairs, whose foundational memoization insight, store each subproblem's answer once, underlies both of these two dimensional string DP problems.

Any problem asking whether two sequences can be merged or reconciled while each preserves its own internal order, where a 2D table over "how much of each sequence has been consumed" is the standard structure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: exponential time, O(n plus m) recursion stack space. Optimized (2D table): O(n times m) time, O(n times m) space. Further optimized (rolling array): O(n times m) time, O(m) space.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a 2D dynamic programming table over positions in s1 and s2, further reduced to a single rolling row.

Core Idea: the recursive backtracking revisits identical (characters consumed from s1, from s2) states repeatedly, so memoizing each pair's answer in a 2D table, filled row by row, computes every state exactly once.
Time: exponential for the brute force, O(n times m) for both dynamic programming versions.
Space: O(n plus m) recursion stack for the brute force, O(n times m) for the full table, O(m) for the rolling row.

Most Important Observation: the position in s3 needing to be matched is always fully determined by how much of s1 and s2 combined have already been consumed, which is exactly what makes the 2D table well defined.
Interview Difficulty: defining the table's meaning correctly and stating the base cases explicitly is the hard part; the rolling array reduction follows naturally once the table version is solid.
One line memory trick: a cell is true if it could have come from s1 above or s2 to the left, matching the right character either way.
